d.title: Four tests you can apply in review
d.caption: 'Pythonic' is a judgement, but each of these is a yes/no question a reviewer can ask of a line of code.

columns.title: Does it use the protocol?
items: for x in xs, not indices

columns.title: Is the intent on the line?

d.title: Module layout, top to bottom
d.caption: The order a reader expects: what this module is, what it needs, what it exports, then the implementation. A module that opens with helper functions makes the reader scroll to find the point.

items.label: public functions and classes
items.sub: in the order a reader needs them

items.label: private helpers
items.sub: _leading underscore, after the code that uses them

d.title: The race that look-before-you-leap cannot fix
d.caption: Between the check and the use, another process can change the world. EAFP does the operation and handles the failure, which closes the gap.

d.title: Unpacking is a length assertion
d.caption: first, *middle, last = seq gives first and last one item each and middle whatever remains — an empty list for a two-item sequence. Without the star, the counts must match exactly or Python raises.
d.label: first, *middle, last = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]   → first=1, middle=[2, 3, 4], last=5

d.title: The pattern kinds
d.caption: A case clause is a pattern that either matches the subject's shape and binds names, or fails and falls through to the next case. Patterns nest, so a mapping pattern can contain a sequence pattern that contains a class pattern.

d.title: Iterable versus iterator
d.caption: An iterable knows how to make an iterator (__iter__); an iterator produces values (__next__) and is exhausted once. A list is iterable and reusable; a generator is an iterator and one-shot.

d.title: A generator pipeline pulls one item at a time
d.caption: Nothing runs until the consumer asks. Each stage yields one item to the next; no stage ever holds the whole dataset, so a ten-gigabyte file streams through in constant memory.

d.title: What `with` guarantees
d.caption: __enter__ runs, the block runs, and __exit__ runs no matter how the block ends — normally, by return, by break, or by an exception. That is the whole contract, and it is why files close and locks release.

items.label: cm = expr; value = cm.__enter__()
items.desc: the 'as' name is bound to __enter__'s return

items.label: the block runs
items.desc: return, break, continue, or an exception can all leave it

items.label: cm.__exit__(type, value, tb)
items.desc: always runs; receives the exception if there was one

items.label: exception re-raised unless __exit__ returned True
items.desc: suppressing is a decision, and usually the wrong one

d.title: deque: O(1) at both ends
d.caption: A deque is a doubly linked block list. appendleft and popleft are O(1) where a list's insert(0) and pop(0) are O(n); maxlen turns it into a rolling window that drops the oldest item automatically.
d.label: deque(maxlen=4): a fifth append drops 'a' from the left

d.title: groupby groups consecutive equal keys only
d.caption: groupby does not sort. Adjacent runs of the same key become one group; a key that reappears later starts a new group. Sort by the key first if you want one group per key.
d.label: groupby('aabaac') → ('a', 2), ('b', 1), ('a', 2), ('c', 1) — four groups, not three

d.title: Before reaching for a regex
d.caption: Most string questions have a method that is faster, clearer and impossible to get catastrophically wrong. The regex is the fourth option, not the first.

items.label: str methods
items.desc: startswith, endswith, split, partition, strip, isdigit

items.label: in and find
items.desc: substring tests and positions

items.label: a real parser
items.desc: json, csv, urllib.parse, email — structured formats have libraries

items.label: re — a compiled, commented, tested pattern
items.desc: when the shape is genuinely a pattern

d.title: Catastrophic backtracking
d.caption: (a+)+ against 'aaaa…b' tries every way of splitting the a's between the inner and outer groups before failing — 2ⁿ attempts. Possessive quantifiers, atomic groups or a rewritten pattern remove the ambiguity.

d.title: Three passes over a script
d.caption: Correctness first, then the seams that make it testable, then what production needs. Doing them in this order means each pass has something stable to work on.

items.label: Pass 1 — correctness
items.desc: the mutable default, the bare except, the wrong encoding, the off-by-one

items.label: Pass 2 — seams
items.desc: pure functions, injected I/O, a main() that takes arguments

items.label: Pass 3 — production
items.desc: logging, config, exit codes, idempotence, a test

d.title: raise unwinds the stack until a handler matches
d.caption: Each frame is checked for a try/except that matches the exception's type; frames without one are discarded on the way up. If nothing matches, the interpreter prints the traceback and exits.

items.label: main()  except ValueError:
items.sub: caught here — execution continues after the try

items.label: the interpreter
items.sub: would print the traceback if nothing had caught it

d.title: The hierarchy is an API
d.caption: Catching a class catches every subclass. except Exception catches almost everything; except BaseException also catches KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit, which is almost never what you want.

d.title: try / except / else / finally
d.caption: except runs only on a matching exception, else only when the try body finished cleanly, finally always. Keeping the success path in else keeps the try block down to the one line that can fail.

nodes.label: try:
nodes.sub: the one call that can fail

d.title: Designing an exception hierarchy
d.caption: One base class per library lets callers catch everything from it in one clause; subclasses let them be specific. Two levels is nearly always enough.

children.label: InvalidAmount
children.sub: a caller bug — do not retry

d.title: Translate at the boundary
d.caption: A low-level exception from a dependency becomes your domain's exception, chained with 'from' so the cause survives in the traceback. Callers see one vocabulary.

nodes.label: except … as e: raise GatewayTimeout(...) from e

d.title: The logging model
d.caption: A logger emits a record; handlers decide where it goes; formatters decide what it looks like; levels filter at each stage. Loggers form a tree by dotted name, and records propagate to the root.

d.title: Levels that mean something
d.caption: A level is a promise about who needs to act. Set the threshold per environment and the meaning per message.

items.label: ERROR
items.sub: a request or job failed; someone should look

items.label: WARNING
items.sub: unexpected but handled; watch the rate

items.label: INFO
items.sub: the normal narrative of the service

d.title: Exponential backoff with jitter
d.caption: Each retry waits roughly twice as long as the last, with random jitter so a thousand clients do not retry in lockstep. Cap the total and give up: a retry is not a fix for a bug.

d.title: A method, not a hunch
d.caption: Reproduce, narrow, hypothesise, test the hypothesis, fix, and add the test that would have caught it. Skipping the reproduction is where most debugging time goes.

items.label: Reproduce
items.desc: a failing test or a one-line script that fails every time

items.label: Narrow
items.desc: bisect the input, the commit, or the code path

items.label: Hypothesise, then check
items.desc: one hypothesis, one experiment — a print or a breakpoint

items.label: Fix, and keep the reproduction
items.desc: the failing test becomes the regression test

d.title: What text mode does
d.caption: open(p) in text mode decodes bytes with an encoding and translates newlines; 'rb' gives you the bytes untouched. Name the encoding every time, because the default depends on the machine.

d.title: Atomic write: temp file, then rename
d.caption: Writing straight into the target leaves a half-written file if the process dies. Write to a temporary file in the same directory, fsync, then rename — the rename is atomic on the same filesystem.

items.label: write to target.tmp
items.desc: same directory, so the rename cannot cross filesystems

items.label: flush and os.fsync()
items.desc: the bytes are on disk, not in a cache

items.label: os.replace('target.tmp', 'target')
items.desc: atomic: readers see the old file or the new one, never a partial

d.title: JSON's type map
d.caption: JSON has six types; Python has more. Everything that is not in the table needs a default= encoder on the way out and a conversion on the way in — datetimes, Decimals, sets and dataclasses included.

d.title: A pickle is an instruction stream
d.caption: pickle.loads runs a small stack machine whose opcodes can import any module and call any callable. Unpickling data you did not produce is executing code you did not write.

nodes.label: pickle bytes
nodes.sub: from a file or the network

d.title: What import actually does
d.caption: A module is executed exactly once and cached in sys.modules; every later import anywhere in the process returns the same module object. That cache is also what makes circular imports fail halfway.

items.label: sys.modules['pkg.mod'] cached?
items.desc: yes → bind the name and stop

items.label: find it: sys.path, finders, loaders
items.desc: a .py, a package directory, a compiled extension

items.label: create the module object and register it
items.desc: in sys.modules before executing — so cycles see a partial module

items.label: execute the module body top to bottom
items.desc: def and class statements run; side effects happen here

d.title: A circular import
d.caption: a imports b at the top; b imports a at the top; when b runs, a is in sys.modules but half-executed, so from a import thing fails with ImportError. Move the import inside the function, or move the shared thing to a third module.

d.title: The src layout
d.caption: The package lives under src/, so tests import the installed package rather than the working directory by accident. pyproject.toml at the root describes how to build and install it.

d.title: Direct versus transitive dependencies
d.caption: You declare the direct ones; the resolver pulls in their dependencies. A lock file records every resolved version so two installs on two machines are identical.

d.title: From source to a published package
d.caption: The build backend named in pyproject.toml turns the source tree into an sdist and a wheel; twine or uv uploads them; pip resolves and installs the wheel on the other side.

d.title: Naive and aware datetimes
d.caption: A naive datetime has no zone and means nothing until you attach one; an aware one carries a tzinfo. Store and compare in UTC; convert to a local zone only at the edge.

d.title: send() makes a generator two-way
d.caption: A value passed to send() becomes the result of the yield expression inside the generator. The first call must be send(None) to advance to the first yield.

d.title: A decorator with arguments is three functions deep
d.caption: @retry(times=3) calls retry(3) first, which returns the actual decorator, which receives the function and returns the wrapper. Each layer closes over the one outside it.

items.label: retry(times=3)
items.sub: the factory: runs at decoration, returns decorator

items.label: wrapper(*args, **kwargs)
items.sub: runs on every call; sees times and func

d.title: Annotations are inert at runtime
d.caption: The interpreter stores annotations and never checks them. mypy or pyright reads the same annotations before the code runs; Pydantic and FastAPI read them at runtime to validate. Three consumers, one syntax.

d.title: Variance, on list and Sequence
d.caption: list is invariant: a list[Dog] is not a list[Animal], because the callee could append a Cat. Sequence is covariant: read-only, so the substitution is safe. Callable is contravariant in its arguments.

columns.title: contravariant · Callable[[T], R]
items: a handler of Animal accepts Dog

d.title: Attribute lookup, with descriptors
d.caption: The full order behind obj.x: data descriptors on the type win, then the instance dict, then non-data descriptors and plain class attributes. property is a data descriptor; a function is a non-data descriptor, which is why methods bind.

items.label: type(obj).__mro__ has a data descriptor 'x'?
items.desc: __set__ or __delete__ defined — property, slots — call its __get__

items.label: 'x' in obj.__dict__?
items.desc: return the instance value

items.label: non-data descriptor or class attribute?
items.desc: functions bind here: func.__get__(obj, type) → bound method

items.label: __getattr__(name) if defined
items.desc: else AttributeError

d.title: What a class statement does
d.caption: The body runs as a function to fill a namespace, then the metaclass — type unless you say otherwise — is called with the name, bases and namespace to build the class object. Hooks fire along the way.

items.label: determine the metaclass
items.desc: from the bases and any metaclass= keyword

items.label: metaclass.__prepare__(name, bases)
items.desc: the namespace the body will fill — usually a dict

items.label: execute the class body
items.desc: def and assignments populate the namespace

items.label: cls = metaclass(name, bases, namespace)
items.desc: __new__ and __init__ of the metaclass; __set_name__ on descriptors; __init_subclass__ on the parent

d.title: Stack frames, as inspect sees them
d.caption: inspect.stack() returns the frames from the current one outward; each carries its code object, locals, line number and the caller. Reading frames is how debuggers, loggers with caller info and tracebacks work.

d.title: Reference counting
d.caption: Every object carries a count of the names and containers that refer to it. When the count reaches zero the object is freed immediately — no collector involved. sys.getrefcount reports one extra for its own argument.

d.title: A reference cycle that counting cannot free
d.caption: a.partner = b and b.partner = a: each keeps the other's count at one even after every outside name is gone. The generational collector finds such cycles and frees them; weakref breaks them at the source.

d.title: The five-step leak workflow
d.caption: Confirm the growth, find the allocating line, find the accumulating type, find who holds the reference, then fix. Each step has one tool.

items.label: Confirm memory is growing
items.desc: psutil RSS over time — growth that never plateaus

items.label: Find what line allocates it
items.desc: tracemalloc snapshots, compared

items.label: Find which type accumulates
items.desc: gc.get_objects() counts, objgraph.show_most_common_types

items.label: Find who holds the reference
items.desc: objgraph.show_backrefs on one instance

items.label: Fix it
items.desc: a cache without a bound, a handler never removed, a closure in a global, a cycle with __del__
